youtube_title: Who Really Killed Sakamoto Ryoma? The Evidence Pointed at the Shinsengumi — Then a Man Confessed
youtube_description:
The morning after Sakamoto Ryoma was cut down at the Omiya inn, his friends held a scabbard, a pair of restaurant clogs and a name: the Shinsengumi. Three years later, a man from a different unit admitted his own unit had been there, and then, thirty years on, changed his story. If you had stood in that street holding the scabbard, would you have named the Shinsengumi too?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. This time he files his dispatch from Kawaramachi Street in Kyoto on the morning of 11 December 1867, the day after the attack. Later testimony (1870, 1900, 1911) is what he read.

I may watch, I may speak, I may not change a thing. Today it sets me down on Kawaramachi Street in Kyoto, at the door of a soy-sauce shop called the Omiya. It is the sixteenth day of the eleventh month, a cold morning; by the calendar I was raised on, the eleventh of December, 1867. Two guests were cut down upstairs last night, and I have come to learn why the men outside already think they know who did it.

scenes.narration: I stand in the doorway with my notebook. The dead man is Sakamoto Ryoma, a man of Tosa. A month ago the shogun did. Last night was the fifteenth of the month, which by the old calendar is Ryoma's birthday. Upstairs, I am told, his friend Nakaoka Shintaro is badly hurt but alive. In the back of the house, a servant is fighting to stay alive.
